'''''Frangula alnus''''', commonly known as '''alder buckthorn''', '''glossy buckthorn''', or '''breaking buckthorn''', is a tall [[deciduous]] shrub in the family [[Rhamnaceae]]. Unlike other "buckthorns", alder buckthorn does not have thorns. It is native to [[Europe]], northernmost [[Africa]], and western [[Asia]], from [[Ireland]] and [[Great Britain]] north to the [[68th parallel north|68th parallel]] in [[Scandinavia]], east to central [[Siberia]] and [[Xinjiang]] in western [[China]], and south to northern [[Morocco]], [[Turkey]], and the [[Alborz]] in [[Iran]] and [[Caucasus Mountains|the Caucasus Mountains]]; in the northwest of its range (Ireland, Scotland), it is rare and scattered. It is also introduced and [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in eastern North America, where it tends to aggressively displace, even outcompete native plant species in forest understories with its seed banks, tolerance of deep shade such as that of late successional forests, and spontaneous, bird-driven recruitment in natural habitats.<ref name="Rushforth">Rushforth, K. (1999). ''Trees of Britain and Europe''. Collins {{ISBN|0-00-220013-9}}.</ref><ref name=fe>Flora Europaea: [http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Frangula&SPECIES_XREF=alnus&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= ''Frangula alnus'']</ref><ref name="Flora">[[Stace, Clive]], et al. ''Interactive Flora of NW Europe'': [http://ip30.eti.uva.nl/BIS/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=3124 ''Frangula alnus'']{{Dead link|date=December 2019 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref><ref name="China">{{eFloras|2|200013382|Rhamnus frangula |family=Rhamnaceae |first1=Yilin |last1=Chen |first2=Carsten |last2=Schirarend}}</ref>

== Description ==
[[File:Frangula-alnus-buds-2010-02-11.jpg|thumb|Winter shoot with buds]]
Alder buckthorn is a non-spiny deciduous shrub, growing to {{convert|3|–|6|m|ft|0|abbr=on}}, occasionally to {{convert|7|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall. It is usually multistemmed but rarely forms a small tree with a trunk diameter of up to {{convert|20|cm|in|0|abbr=on}}. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is dark blackish-brown, with bright lemon-yellow inner bark exposed if cut. The shoots are dark brown, the winter buds without bud scales, protected only by the densely hairy outer leaves.

The leaves are arranged [[alternate leaf|alternately]] on {{convert|8|–|15|mm|in|frac=32|adj=on|abbr=off}} [[petiole (botany)|petioles]]. They are [[Glossary of leaf morphology#ovate|ovate]], {{convert|3|–|7|cm|in|frac=4|abbr=on}} long by {{convert|2.5|–|4|cm|in|frac=8|abbr=on}} wide (rarely to {{convert|11|cm|in|disp=or|frac=4|abbr=on}} by {{convert|6|cm|in|disp=or|frac=4|abbr=on}}). They have 6–10 pairs of prominently grooved and slightly downy veins and an [[entire margin]].

The [[flower]]s are small, {{convert|3|–|5|mm|in|frac=32|abbr=in}} in diameter, star-shaped with five greenish-white acute triangular [[petal]]s, [[hermaphroditic (botany)|hermaphroditic]], and [[insect-pollinated]], flowering in May to June in clusters of two to ten in the [[leaf axil]]s.

The [[fruit]] is a small black [[Berry (botany)|berry]] {{convert|6|–|10|mm|in|frac=32|abbr=in}} in diameter, ripening from green through red in late summer to dark purple or black in early autumn, containing two or three pale brown {{convert|5|mm|in|frac=32|adj=on|abbr=off}} [[seed]]s. The seeds are primarily dispersed by [[frugivorous]] birds, which readily eat the fruit.<ref name="Rushforth" /><ref name="Flora" /><ref name="China" /><ref name="Natural" /><ref name="Blamey">Blamey, M. & Grey-Wilson, C. (1989). ''Flora of Britain and Northern Europe''. {{ISBN|0-340-40170-2}}.</ref> Its fruit [[persistence (botany)|persists]] for an average of 15.3 days, and bears an average of 2.0 seeds per fruit. Fruits average 86.2% water, and their [[dry matter|dry weight]] includes 25.0% [[carbohydrate]]s and 0.5% [[lipid]]s.{{sfn|Ehrlén|Eriksson|1991}}

== Taxonomy and naming ==
[[File:Rhamnus frangula 07 ies.jpg|thumb|Flowering shoot]]
Alder buckthorn was first formally described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753 as ''Rhamnus frangula''. It was subsequently separated by [[Philip Miller]] in 1768 into the genus ''Frangula'' on the basis of its hermaphrodite flowers with a five-parted corolla (in ''Rhamnus'' the flowers are dioecious and four-parted); this restored the treatment of pre-Linnaean authors, notably [[Joseph Pitton de Tournefort|Tournefort]].<ref>Miller, P. (1754). ''The Gardener's Dictionary'', 8th ed. [http://www.botanicus.org/page/394932 Facsimile at Botanicus.org]</ref> Although much disputed historically, the separation of ''Frangula'' from ''Rhamnus'' is now widely accepted, being supported by recent genetic data<ref>Bolmgren, K., & Oxelman, B. 2004. [http://kjellbolmgren.net/publications_files/Bolmgren_%26_Oxelman_Taxon_2004.pdf Generic limits in Rhamnus L. s.l. (Rhamnaceae) inferred from nuclear and chloroplast DNA sequence phylogenies.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110819120327/http://kjellbolmgren.net/publications_files/Bolmgren_%26_Oxelman_Taxon_2004.pdf |date=2011-08-19 }} ''Taxon'' 53: 383–390.</ref> though a few authorities still retain the genus within ''Rhamnus'' (e.g., the ''Flora of China''<ref name="China" />).

The genus name ''Frangula'', from [[Latin]] {{wikt-lang|la|frango}} "to break", refers to the brittle wood. Both the common name alder buckthorn and specific epithet ''alnus'' refer to its association with [[alder]]s (''Alnus'') on damp sites. Unlike other "buckthorns", alder buckthorn does not have thorns.<ref name="Vedel">Vedel, H., & Lange, J. (1960). ''Trees and Bushes in Wood and Hedgerow''. Methuen & Co Ltd.</ref><ref name="Natural">Natural England: [http://www.plantpress.com/wildlife/search.php?name=Frangula&pl=5&adv=1&ot=&r=0&g=0&p=1&o=481 Alder buckthorn] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110720013443/http://www.plantpress.com/wildlife/search.php?name=Frangula&pl=5&adv=1&ot=&r=0&g=0&p=1&o=481 |date=2011-07-20 }}</ref> Other recorded names include glossy buckthorn and breaking buckthorn; historically, it was sometimes called "dogwood" through confusion of the leaves with those of [[Cornus sanguinea|dogwood]] ''Cornus sanguinea''.<ref name="Vedel" />

== Ecology ==
Alder buckthorn grows in wet soils in open woods, scrub, hedgerows and bogs, thriving well in sunlight and moderate shade, but less vigorously in dense shade; it prefers acidic soils though will also grow on neutral soils.<ref name="Flora" /><ref name="Vedel" /><ref name="Blamey" />

''Frangula alnus'' is one of just two food plants (the other being ''[[Rhamnus cathartica]]'') used by the [[common brimstone]] butterfly (''Gonepteryx rhamni''). The flowers are valuable for [[bee]]s, and the fruit an important food source for birds, particularly [[thrush (bird)|thrushes]].<ref name="Natural" />
[[File:Alder buckthorn in Brede High Wood - geograph.org.uk - 5278210.jpg|thumb|Alder buckthorn in East Sussex, England]]

=== Invasive species ===
''Frangula alnus'' was probably introduced to [[North America]] about 200 years ago, and in Canada about 100 years ago. It was planted for hedgerows, forestry plantings, and wildlife habitat, but has become an [[invasive species]], invading forests in the northeastern [[United States]] and wetlands and moist forest in the Midwestern United States.<ref name="Wingard">{{cite web | url = http://gradworks.umi.com/14/43/1443642.html | author = Wingard, Hanna S | title = Invasion of transition hardwood forests by exotic Rhamnus frangula: Chronology and site requirements | publisher = University of New Hampshire, 2007}}</ref><ref name="Maine">{{cite web | url = http://www.umext.maine.edu/onlinepubs/htmpubs/2505.htm | title = Common Buckthorn and Glossy Buckthorn | publisher = University of Maine Cooperative Extension Bulletin #2505 | access-date = 2009-10-02 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20090714223737/http://www.umext.maine.edu/onlinepubs/htmpubs/2505.htm | archive-date = 2009-07-14 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.invasive.org/species/subject.cfm?sub=5649 | title = glossy buckthorn | publisher = Invasive.org: Center for Invasive Species and Ecosystem Health}}</ref> It is predicted to continue to expand its North American range with time.<ref name="Wingard" /> Its invasiveness is assisted by its high adaptability and pollution tolerance.<ref name="Newhampshire">{{cite web | url = http://extension.unh.edu/forestry/Docs/invasive.pdf | title = Guide to invasive upland plant species in New Hampshire | publisher = New Hampshire Department of Agriculture, Markets & Food Terrestrial Invasive Plant Species, page 14 | access-date = 2009-10-02 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20080828032739/http://extension.unh.edu/forestry/Docs/invasive.pdf | archive-date = 2008-08-28 }}</ref> It is one of three species of buckthorn that occurs without cultivation in eastern Canada.<ref>Catling, P.M., and Z.S. Porebski. 1994. The history of invasion and current status of glossy buckthorn, ''Rhamnus frangula'', in Southern Ontario. Canadian Field-Naturalist 108:305–310</ref>

It invades forests and grows in the understory in spots with a lot of light. These areas, usually where a tree has fallen, normally allow locally native tree seedlings to grow and eventually fill in the gap in the canopy. But when ''Frangula alnus'' invades and grows in these locations, its dense canopy prevents light from reaching the ground and therefore prevents other seedlings from growing.<ref name="Newhampshire" /> It tends to grow more densely and with larger individuals in lower topographical areas with moist, fertile soils, and is very problematic for land managers in areas where it is non-native. Uplands forests are not invaded as easily as lower lying ones. [[Tsuga|Hemlock]]-[[oak]] stands, which tend to be older stands of trees, are much less suitable for ''Frangula alnus'' because the density of the tree canopy creates a more shady environment that is not as suitable for ''Frangula alnus''. [[Eastern white pine]] stands are easily invaded because they allow more light to reach the [[forest floor]], and tree stands that are cut are very quickly invaded while undisturbed stands are rarely invaded.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Chelsea Cunard and Thomas D. Lee | title = Is patience a virtue? Succession, light, and the death of invasive glossy buckthorn (''Frangula alnus'') | journal = Biological Invasions | year = 2009 | volume = 11 | issue = 3 | pages = 577–586 | publisher = Biological Invasions:Volume 11, Number 3 / March, 2009| doi = 10.1007/s10530-008-9272-8 | bibcode = 2009BiInv..11..577C | s2cid = 23517872 }}</ref>

V. |date=August 1991 |title=Egg-Laying Requirements of Woodland Butterflies; Brimstones (Gonepteryx rhamni) and Alder Buckthorn (Frangula alnus) |journal=The Journal of Applied Ecology |volume=28 |issue=2 |pages=731–743 |doi=10.2307/2404579 |jstor=2404579 |bibcode=1991JApEc..28..731M |issn=0021-8901}}</ref> Compared to other populations of ''Frangula alnus'', the population in Ireland also has lower genetic diversity.<ref name="Finlay-2017" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=RIGUEIRO |first1=C. |last2=ARROYO |first2=J. M. |last3=RODRÍGUEZ |first3=R. |last4=HAMPE |first4=A. |last5=JORDANO |first5=P. |date=May 2009 |title=Isolation and characterization of 16 polymorphic microsatellite loci forFrangula alnus(Rhamnaceae) |journal=Molecular Ecology Resources |volume=9 |issue=3 |pages=986–989 |doi=10.1111/j.1755-0998.2009.02527.x |pmid=21564814 |bibcode=2009MolER...9..986R |s2cid=15974997 |issn=1755-098X|hdl=10261/38390 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==== Control ====
Small saplings can be hand-pulled, but control of larger examples is best achieved using herbicides.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.dnr.state.mn.us/invasives/terrestrialplants/woody/buckthorn/control.html | title = What you can do to control buckthorn! | work = Minnesota Department of Natural Resources | publisher = MN Department of Natural Resources}}</ref> ''Frangula alnus'' and the related species ''[[Rhamnus cathartica]]'' have been banned from sale, transport, or import to [[Minnesota]]<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.dnr.state.mn.us/invasives/terrestrialplants/woody/buckthorn/index.html | title = Buckthorn | work = Minnesota Department of Natural Resources | publisher = MN Department of Natural Resources}}</ref> and [[Illinois]].<ref>{{cite web | url = http://dnr.state.il.us/pubaffairs/mp3~file~instructions.htm | publisher = Illinois Department of Natural Resources | date = April 22, 2004 | title = Reminder to Gardeners: Some Exotic Plants Banned in Illinois | access-date = February 7, 2010 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20110608195444/http://dnr.state.il.us/pubaffairs/mp3~file~instructions.htm | archive-date = June 8, 2011 }}</ref> It is considered invasive, but not banned, in [[Connecticut]].<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.hort.uconn.edu/CIPWG/invplantsCT09commonname.pdf | title = Connecticut Invasive Plant List July 2009 | publisher = CT Invasive Plants Council}}</ref>

== Cultivation and uses ==

=== Decorative ===
[[File:Frangula-alnus-asplenifolia-autumn.jpg|thumb|right|''Frangula alnus'' 'Asplenifolia' with autumn colours]]
Alder buckthorn has limited decorative qualities without conspicuous flowers or bold foliage, and is mainly grown for its conservation value, particularly to attract Brimstone butterflies. A [[variegated]] cultivar ''Frangula alnus'' 'Variegata' and a cultivar with very slender leaves 'Asplenifolia' are sometimes grown in gardens as ornamental shrubs. The cultivar 'Tallhedge' has been selected for hedging.<ref name="Future">{{PFAF}}</ref>

=== Medicinal ===
[[Galen]], a Greek physician of the 2nd century AD, knew of alder buckthorn, although he did not distinguish clearly in his writings between it and other closely related species. All of these plants though, were credited with the power to protect against witchcraft, demons, poisons, and headaches.{{citation needed|date=September 2010}}

The bark (and to a lesser extent the fruit) has been used as a [[laxative]], due to its 3–7% [[Natural anthraquinone|anthraquinone]] content. Bark for medicinal use is dried and stored for a year before use, as fresh bark is violently purgative; even dried bark can be dangerous if taken in excess.<ref name="Rushforth" /><ref name="Future" />

=== Other uses ===
Alder buckthorn charcoal is prized in the manufacture of [[gunpowder]], being regarded as the best wood for the purpose. It is particularly highly valued for time fuses because of its very even burn rate.<ref name="Rushforth" /><ref name="Vedel" /> The wood was formerly used for [[shoe last]]s, nails, and veneer. The bark yields a yellow dye, and the unripe berries furnish a green dye.<ref name="Future" />
